items.item: Minimal/full response detail split on /encrypt, /decrypt, and their batch endpoints
items.notes: Prompted by an explicit design call: since this service has never had a real external consumer yet, deprecated/informational fields have no backward-compatibility meaning to preserve -- so the three legacy binary fields on EncryptResponse (ivB64/ciphertextB64/tagB64, superseded by the ciphertext token) were deleted outright rather than merely hidden, and the informational/audit fields (edek_id, owner_app_id, algorithm, encoding on encrypt, kek_version) were made opt-in instead of always-on. New minimal (default) vs full (opt-in via X-Response-Detail: full request header) view via Jackson @JsonView, gated by a new global ResponseDetailBodyAdvice (com.hsm.core.web) covering EncryptResponse/DecryptResponse/BatchEncryptResponse/BatchDecryptResponse; decrypt's encoding field stays in minimal since it's functionally required to interpret plaintext. Legacy iv_b64/ciphertext_b64/tag_b64 remain accepted as request-side input (DecryptRequest/BatchDecryptItem, unrelated to the deleted response fields). Demo UI (app.js) now always sends X-Response-Detail: full so its field-breakdown panel keeps showing every field. Non-trivial porting cost: Spring Boot 4/Spring Framework 7 moved to Jackson 3, which silently broke the pre-existing MappingJacksonValue-based view-selection convention (throws UnsupportedOperationException, 'use hints instead') -- the real mechanism moved to ResponseBodyAdvice.determineWriteHints, and Jackson 3 also flipped MapperFeature.DEFAULT_VIEW_INCLUSION's default from true to false, meaning every field on a viewed type now needs an explicit @JsonView annotation or it silently vanishes the moment any view is active for that type (bit both the top-level DTOs and, one level deeper, the batch wrapper/result-item DTOs). Root-caused via decompiling Spring/Jackson bytecode (javap), not documentation, since this is newly-introduced-by-the-upgrade behavior. Verified: full reactor test suite (59/59 hsm-core-service tests, 0 regressions), live curl against all 4 endpoints in both views, and a live browser check that the demo UI's field-breakdown panel still renders correctly.

items.item: Run the Gatling load test against a deployed hsm-core-service, not just demo mode
items.notes: Follow-up to the Gatling harness above -- that harness only ever ran against localhost demo mode; this round adds two ways to point the exact same EncryptDecryptLoadSimulation at a real deployed instance instead, no new simulation class. (1) hsm-core-service/scripts/run-load-test-k8s.sh: kubectl port-forwards the deployed Service then delegates to run-load-test.sh with -Dhsm.baseUrl/-Dhsm.appId/-Dhsm.token pointed at the tunnel -- zero new infra, produces the same interactive HTML report, but port-forward is a proxying hop (inflates absolute latency) and is capped by the local machine's own network stack. (2) helm/hsm-core-service-loadtest-job + java/docker/Dockerfile.hsm-core-service-loadtest: packages the simulation as a one-shot in-cluster Job, mirroring helm/hsm-bulk-client-job's existing pattern -- more representative numbers, no port-forward hop, but real new infra to build/push. Both surfaced a real requirement change from the local-demo-mode run: deployed hsm-core-service runs DEMO_MODE=false/RsaJwtValidator, so MockJwtValidator's fixed demo-token-* strings don't work -- both paths require a real app_id + bearer JWT (the Job sources these from a Secret via $(HSM_APP_ID)/$(HSM_TOKEN) env-var references, never a plain values.yaml string, same credential-handling standard as this repo's other charts). Also confirmed no Ingress exists in helm/hsm-core-service's chart (Service only, ClusterIP) -- port-forward is the only way to reach a deployed instance from outside the cluster today. The Job image needed a real fix, not just Docker boilerplate: distroless has no shell, so all per-run tuning (-Dhsm.baseUrl/-Dhsm.appId/-Dhsm.token/-Dhsm.singleUsers/etc.) has to arrive via the JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS env var (auto-consumed by the JVM before main()) rather than a wrapper entrypoint script; and a bare `java -cp ... io.gatling.app.Gatling` invocation needed --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED added explicitly -- gatling-maven-plugin sets this automatically when it forks its own JVM (confirmed in mvn's own launcher script), so the failure (IllegalAccessException on Gatling's stats writer) only ever surfaces once you leave the Maven-plugin path, reproduced live before fixing it. Also chose not to fight the no-shell constraint for report retrieval: kubectl cp needs tar inside the target container, which distroless doesn't have, so the in-cluster Job's results are read via kubectl logs (Gatling's own console summary) rather than the HTML report -- documented as the real tradeoff against the port-forward path in java/docs/PERFORMANCE_TESTING.md, not silently worked around. Validated: the copy-dependencies build step, the exact ENTRYPOINT invocation (found and fixed the --add-opens gap live against local demo mode), and helm lint/template on the new chart (including its required(...) guards on targetSecretName/baseUrl failing closed correctly) -- the actual port-forward-against-a-real-Service and real-cluster Job run are not live-verified, no Kubernetes cluster reachable in this environment (same limitation as every other Helm chart in this repo).

items.item: hsm-bulk-client: multi-database source/target support (SQL Server, Azure SQL, Oracle)
items.notes: Real requirement, not speculative -- consumers' own source/target databases are MS SQL Server/Azure SQL Database (wire-compatible with on-prem SQL Server, one dialect to build) and Oracle, not just Postgres. Scoped in an explicit requirements discussion before writing code: this round is dialect support only; letting a source be an arbitrary SQL query instead of a whole table (for callers needing only a filtered subset) was raised in the same discussion and deliberately deferred. New DbDialect enum (POSTGRESQL/SQL_SERVER/ORACLE), resolved per connection (source and target independently -- a job can read one vendor and write another) from the JDBC URL scheme, with an explicit override (ClientProperties.Db.TableRef.dialect) that always wins -- added specifically because a URL scheme identifies the wire protocol/driver in use, not necessarily the backend's real SQL dialect quirks (some products present a different vendor's wire protocol for driver compatibility while diverging from that vendor's actual behavior). DbBulkJob's pagination (fetchPage/computePartitionRanges) needed zero per-dialect branching once switched from Postgres's LIMIT shorthand to the ANSI SQL:2008 OFFSET/FETCH clause, which Postgres/SQL Server 2012+/Oracle 12c+ all support natively -- only CheckpointStore (existence check, DDL, MERGE/ON CONFLICT upsert) has genuine per-vendor SQL, since Postgres's to_regclass/ON CONFLICT have no equivalent on the other two. SQL Server's MERGE-requires-a-terminating-semicolon requirement and Oracle's MERGE...USING(SELECT :a AS a FROM dual) multi-bind pattern were both confirmed against Microsoft Learn/Oracle's own official docs before being written, not guessed. New mssql-jdbc:13.4.0.jre11 and ojdbc17:23.26.3.0.0 dependencies, both confirmed on Maven Central under an open license (no private repo/credentials needed). Verified live against real H2 (a new PaginationSyntaxTest, 5/5 passing) that the exact ANSI OFFSET/FETCH SQL text is correct -- H2 deliberately chosen as a second real engine corroborating Postgres/SQL Server/Oracle's own documented syntax is genuinely standard. New CheckpointStoreTest (Testcontainers: real Postgres/SQL Server/Oracle) covers ensureTable/save/clear per dialect -- not run in this environment (no reachable Docker daemon), but along the way found and fixed a real gap: a bare @Testcontainers/@Container class hard-fails mvn test rather than skipping when no Docker daemon is reachable, which would have broken this module's default build in any Docker-less environment; fixed with @EnabledIfDockerAvailable, confirmed live that the class now skips cleanly (0 failures, 3 skipped) instead of failing. mvn --fail-at-end test across the full reactor: hsm-bulk-client SUCCESS; the only reactor failure was hsm-core-service's pre-existing, unrelated DemoProfileContextLoadTest H2-lock error from a demo instance left running earlier in the same session.

items.item: Multi-KEK support: kek_registry, self-sufficient EdekRecord, rekey/reversion
items.notes: Prompted by a code review comment: each purpose should be its own KEK, not one global key for the whole service. New kek_registry table (V11 migration) resolves (app_id, dek_name) -> kek_name via a 3-tier fallback: exact dek_name match, then data_classification match, then per-app default, then the legacy single-KEK config value if nothing is registered at all (the one deliberate exception to fail-closed, since every existing app would otherwise break the moment this table exists with zero rows). edek_records gained kek_name (NULL on pre-migration rows, meaning the legacy default) plus previous_kek_name/previous_kek_version/previous_edek_blob -- a single-level undo buffer, not a history table, since the unbounded historical trail already belongs in AuditLogger, not a growing DB row per rotation. KekClient's interface changed to wrapDek(dek, kekName)/unwrapDek(edek, kekName, kekVersion) -- deliberately still knows nothing about app_id/dek_name/kek_registry, that resolution stays a KekRegistryService concern. RotationService redesigned: rotateKek() now groups by the distinct kek_name values actually present in edek_records (not kek_registry, since a KEK can still have live EDEKs after kek_registry stops pointing new writes at it) and rotates each group to its own current version; new rekey(fromKekName, toKekName) and revertRekey(kekName) admin operations move/restore EDEKs between KEKs in place using the undo buffer, each firing a dedicated AuditLogger event. New admin endpoints POST /admin/rekey-kek and /admin/rekey-kek/revert. Found and fixed along the way: a Flyway migration-file version collision with an unrelated V8 already in db/migration-demo (renumbered to V11 -- the demo profile combines both Flyway locations into one shared version namespace, so a same-numbered migration in each location genuinely collides, contradicting an earlier assumption that the two locations were independently versioned), and a Spring Data derived-query ambiguity (findDistinctKekNameByRotationStatusAndKekNameIsNotNull silently projected whole entities instead of just the column, since the parser couldn't disambiguate the same property name appearing as both the projection and an And-clause predicate -- fixed with an explicit @Query). Verified: full hsm-core-service test suite (68/68) passing, plus live end-to-end against a running demo instance -- encrypt/decrypt survives a grouped rotate-kek, a rekey to a second named KEK, and a revert-rekey back, each confirmed by decrypting the same ciphertext token after every step.

items.item: hsm-bulk-service merged into hsm-core-service: single codebase, deployment-level isolation preserved
items.notes: Retired hsm-bulk-service as a separate Maven module/codebase; POST /dek/issue and POST /dek/unwrap are now endpoints on hsm-core-service itself, reusing its single KekClient/edek_records/RotationService/AuditLogger instead of duplicated com.hsm.bulk.* copies. Motivated by two threads converging: (1) the original case for a separate binary -- keeping raw-key-adjacent capability structurally out of the primary service -- didn't actually hold up, since /dek/issue exposes no more than /encrypt already does through the same KekClient boundary; multi-KEK support (added in the same round) confirmed a merge doesn't collapse any key-security blast radius, since that's governed by kek_registry/RBAC-per-key regardless of which process handles a request. (2) hsm-bulk-service was meant to be dormant (scaled to zero between onboarding/de-boarding windows), which made it structurally unable to reliably own the *scheduled* rotation responsibility for the very EDEKs it minted -- those rows outlive the bulk-issuance burst that created them. The deployment-level traffic isolation that was the real reason for a separate process is preserved instead: helm/hsm-bulk-service's chart now deploys the identical hsm-core-service image as a second, independently-scaled release (bulk traffic can still be routed to and scaled separately from ordinary /encrypt//decrypt traffic), rather than a separate codebase. Dockerfile.hsm-bulk-service retired outright. Concrete merge work: ported TransportWrapper + 8 DTOs + DekIssueService/DekUnwrapService/DekController into com.hsm.core.*, adapted for the new kekName-aware KekClient and KekRegistryService resolution; added AppRegistration.publicKeyPem (column existed since V6, JPA field didn't) and AppRegistryService.getPublicKey(); added hsm.service.dek-batch-max-items config and a Hikari pool-size bump (DB_POOL_MAX_SIZE, default 20) carried over from hsm-bulk-service's own tuning; did NOT port hsm-bulk-service's own NamedDekRotationScheduler, since hsm-core-service's existing one already sweeps every named EDEK regardless of which endpoint minted it -- running both would have meant two schedulers racing over the same rows. Updated hsm-bulk-client's default svc.base-url and all config-examples from port 3006 to 3005; rewrote CoreBulkFileInteropTest to spawn one hsm-core-service process instead of two. Verified: full reactor compiles and tests pass (hsm-core-service 68/68, including 2 ported DekIssue/DekUnwrap service tests), and a live end-to-end run against a running instance -- /dek/issue, /dek/unwrap, /encrypt, /decrypt, /admin/rotate-kek, /admin/rekey-kek, and /admin/rekey-kek/revert all exercised for real, including decrypting the same ciphertext token across a rotate-kek and a rekey/revert-rekey cycle.

items.item: Self-issued bearer JWT authentication + POST /admin/apps/keys key provisioning
items.notes: Built for legacy callers that find Entra ID client-credentials/JWT-renewal machinery operationally painful but can manage a one-time RSA keypair (same operational shape as an SSH key) -- 'renewal' becomes pure local computation (re-sign a small JWT), never a network call to an external IdP. New V12 migration adds app_registrations.signing_public_key_pem, independent of the pre-existing public_key_pem (DEK-transport key) -- NULL is a deliberate legacy switch, not just unset: an app with only one key registered gets that same key used for signature verification too, for callers that would rather manage one keypair than two; modern callers register both. New SelfSignedAppKeyJwtValidator verifies a caller-signed RFC-7523-style assertion against the app's registered signing key, with a server-enforced 5-minute max TTL (the caller fully controls its own claims, unlike an Entra-ID-issued token, so this can't be left to the token alone). New SelfIssuedRoutingJwtValidator wraps whichever primary validator the mode calls for (MockJwtValidator in demo, RsaJwtValidator in production) and routes each request by peeking its *unverified* iss claim before trusting anything in it -- never a blind try-both chain: iss matching the configured Entra ID issuer goes to the primary validator, anything else (including every demo-mode literal token, which isn't JWT-shaped at all) goes to the self-signed path. New POST /admin/apps/keys endpoint provisions/rotates either or both keys, validating each PEM at write time (422 on malformed input, not a later failure at first use) and firing an app_keys_updated audit event -- replaces the earlier no-admin-endpoint direct-SQL workaround. Gated by a new, deliberately separate scope (provision_app_keys, not manage_apps): this key is now part of the authentication trust boundary, not just DEK confidentiality, a meaningfully bigger blast radius than the existing active/inactive toggle -- reusing manage_apps was considered and explicitly rejected in favor of the narrower grant, with the option to fold the two together later if that scope split proves unnecessary in practice (a config-only, fully reversible change either direction, since hasAnyAuthority(...) accepts multiple scopes on one access-rule). Client-side counterpart: new SelfSignedJwtTokenProvider (hsm-crypto-client), a third TokenProvider alongside Static/AzureAd, caching the signed token and re-signing only within 15s of its own 2-minute TTL. Verified live end-to-end against a running instance: a self-signed JWT signed with the registered signing key succeeded on /dek/issue (using the *separately* registered encryption key for the actual DEK wrap, confirming the two keys are genuinely independent); a JWT signed with the wrong key was correctly rejected with 401 Invalid token signature; the pre-existing static demo-token path kept working unchanged. Full reactor test suite unaffected.

items.item: New module hsm-crypto-client: embeddable HsmCryptoClient for JVM applications to import directly
items.notes: Answers a distinct requirement from hsm-bulk-client's existing config-file batch-job usage: other JVM applications should be able to import a package and call encrypt/decrypt methods directly with their own inputs, owning the client's lifecycle themselves, rather than driving a whole DB/File batch job. SvcClient, TransportWrapper, DekManager, IvFactory, FipsBootstrap, and the TokenProvider family moved out of hsm-bulk-client into this new module verbatim (same package names, so no import changes needed anywhere that already referenced them) -- plain Java, zero Spring dependency, so importing it never drags Spring Boot autoconfiguration/component-scanning into a host application; this is the first genuine inter-module dependency in this repo's Java tree; every other module here still deliberately duplicates rather than shares. ClientProperties.Svc (a nested record with no Spring annotations of its own) extracted to a standalone SvcConfig in the new module for the same reason. New public entry point HsmCryptoClient (stateful, AutoCloseable, builder-configured -- .staticToken(...)/.azureAdToken(...)/.selfSignedJwt(...)): encrypt(bytes)/encrypt(bytes,dekName)/encrypt(bytes,dekName,classification) plus UTF-8 String convenience overloads, all returning the same 'v1....' packed-token format hsm-core-service's own /encrypt produces; decrypt(token) as a single form (the token already carries everything needed). Keeps its own independent encrypt-side (by dekName) and decrypt-side (by edek_id) DEK caches, separate from hsm-bulk-client's own per-run caches -- reusing hsm-bulk-service's already-proven reasoning for why dekName reuse matters (avoiding a fresh /dek/issue round-trip plus an RSA-OAEP unwrap on every call). hsm-bulk-client now depends on this module instead of owning duplicated copies -- DbBulkJob/FileBulkJob are behaviorally unchanged, only their imports moved (ClientProperties.Svc -> SvcConfig, 4 call sites). A real bug surfaced during live verification, not just unit tests: HsmCryptoClient initially threw NoSuchProviderException (BCFIPS) on first use, since BC-FIPS provider registration previously only happened via hsm-bulk-client's own ClientApplication static initializer -- an embedder has no equivalent single entry point, so HsmCryptoClient now registers it in its own static block. Verified live with a standalone program (not hsm-bulk-client itself) importing com.hsm.client.HsmCryptoClient directly against a running hsm-core-service: mint-fresh encrypt/decrypt round trip, dekName reuse across two calls, and full interop with hsm-core-service's own real /decrypt (zero awareness this client exists) -- all passed. Full reactor test suite (all modules) passes with the extraction in place; four Dockerfiles (hsm-core-service, cek-rotation, hsm-core-service-loadtest, hsm-bulk-client) updated to COPY the new module's pom.xml (and, for hsm-bulk-client's own Dockerfile, its src too, since that build now genuinely compiles it via -am rather than just needing its pom.xml present for the reactor to resolve).

items.item: New module hsm-spark-adapter: hsm_encrypt/hsm_decrypt as Spark SQL functions backed by hsm-crypto-client
items.notes: Answers a distinct requirement from hsm-crypto-client's direct-import usage: Spark SQL jobs should be able to call encrypt/decrypt inline in a query (SELECT hsm_encrypt(ssn, 'customers.ssn', 'pii') FROM customers) instead of a host application driving HsmCryptoClient itself. Two registration paths, both backed by the same HsmEncryptUdf/HsmDecryptUdf classes: HsmUdfRegistration.registerAll(spark) (explicit, per-application, built entirely on Spark's stable public UDFRegistration API) and HsmUdfExtension (automatic for every application on a cluster configured with spark.sql.extensions=com.hsm.spark.HsmUdfExtension, reaching into Catalyst-internal SparkSessionExtensions.injectFunction) -- confirmed as Option B (cluster-wide, zero per-application code) over a per-job-only design specifically so ops doesn't need every Spark application's own code touched to get the functions available. Multiple DEKs supported per application, not one function tied to one DEK: dek_name is a per-call SQL argument, not baked into the function at registration time, so one registration serves every column and each column supplies its own dek_name literal (must be a literal constant per column, not a per-row expression, or DEK-reuse caching degrades to a fresh /dek/issue call per row). One appId identity per Spark application (not per job): spark.hsm.appId and the rest of the connection config load once per executor JVM from that application's own Spark conf, lazily on first UDF invocation via a double-checked-locking singleton (HsmCryptoClientHolder) -- required because a Spark UDF gets serialized from driver to executors, so HsmCryptoClient (holding a PrivateKey, HttpClient, and DEK caches) can never be captured directly in a UDF closure; the lazy per-executor-JVM singleton is the same pattern used for JDBC connections/Kafka producers in Spark. The two DEK-transport/signing private keys are always delivered as Secret-mounted file paths (spark.hsm.privateKeyPath/signingKeyPath), never through spark.hsm.* config values or UDF fields, so raw key material never travels through Spark's own config propagation or closure serialization. Built and verified via the same real-jar javap methodology already proven for hsm-crypto-client's BC-FIPS fix: initial build compiled clean against spark-sql_2.12:3.5.1, but the actual target cluster turned out to run Spark 4.x, which javap against a real spark-sql_2.13:4.2.0 jar showed has zero _2.12 releases at all and two genuine Catalyst-internal API breaks versus 3.5.1 -- Column's direct Column(Expression) constructor removed (Spark 4.x's Classic/Connect API unification rebuilt Column on a ColumnNode abstraction instead) and SparkSessionExtensions.injectFunction's Seq parameter changed from scala.collection.Seq to scala.collection.immutable.Seq under Scala 2.13's collections redesign. Fixed by re-pinning to spark-sql_2.13:4.2.0 and bridging Expression<->Column via org.apache.spark.sql.classic.ExpressionUtils.column(...)/.expression(...) (Spark 4.x's own replacement for the removed constructor and the removed Column.expr() accessor) instead of the old direct construction; HsmUdfRegistration's stable-API path needed no changes at all across this version jump. Re-verified via a real mvn compile against the actual 4.2.0 jar after the fix, same as the original 3.5.1 verification. Not yet run against a live Spark cluster in either version -- this sandbox has no JDK capable of executing Spark itself (only JDK 8, too old for this module's bytecode-21 classes, and a JDK 26 build too new for Spark's own Hadoop dependency, which uses Subject.getSubject, removed in JDK 24+) -- flagged explicitly as the verification gap still outstanding before treating this as production-ready. No Docker/Helm changes: the adapter jar is consumed by an external Spark cluster deployment (spark.jars / a container image baked outside this repo / a managed platform's library mechanism), not deployed via this repo's own images or charts.

items.item: hsm-spark-adapter: live-verified against a real Spark 4.2.0 session (not just compiled), two real bugs found and fixed
items.notes: Follow-up to hsm-spark-adapter's initial build: the app team's actual target cluster runs Spark 4.x, not the 3.5.1 this module was first pinned to, so it was re-pinned to spark-sql_2.13:4.2.0 (Spark 4.x publishes no _2.12 artifacts at all) and HsmUdfExtension's Column/Expression bridging was rewritten around Spark 4.x's Classic/Connect API unification, which replaced Column's direct Expression backing with a ColumnNode one -- confirmed via real javap against the actual 4.2.0 jar, same rigor as the original build. That alone only proved compilation, not correctness, so this round went further: got a real local Spark 4.2.0 session actually running, which required first working out which JDK it needs. A Homebrew JDK 26 build -- believed to be the only 'modern' JDK in this sandbox -- fails for Spark 4.2.0, but for a different reason than the JDK-24+/Hadoop-Subject.getSubject issue that blocked the original 3.5.1 attempt (that specific issue is confirmed fixed in Hadoop 3.5.0, the version Spark 4.2.0 bundles, verified by disassembling UserGroupInformation.class and finding zero references to the removed API); JDK 26 instead breaks in spark-unsafe's Platform.<clinit>, which reflects into jdk.internal.ref.Cleaner, an internal class removed by the time JDK 26 shipped -- Spark 4.2.0 simply predates a JDK that new. Turned out a Homebrew openjdk@21 install already existed in this sandbox the whole time (missed earlier because the search only checked /Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines, not Homebrew's keg-only /usr/local/Cellar layout) -- Spark 4.2.0 runs cleanly under it, matching Spark's own documented JDK 17/21 support range. With a working JDK in hand, both registration paths were exercised for real: HsmUdfRegistration.registerAll(spark) and spark.sql.extensions=com.hsm.spark.HsmUdfExtension both register hsm_encrypt/hsm_decrypt into a live SparkSession's catalog, and SELECT hsm_decrypt(...) was actually executed through real SQL parsing, Catalyst analysis, and whole-stage codegen (not interpreted eval) all the way into HsmDecryptUdf.call(), surfacing the exact expected IllegalStateException for a missing spark.hsm.baseUrl conf -- proof the full chain works, not just that it compiles. That live run caught two real bugs in HsmUdfExtension, neither a Spark-3-vs-4 difference -- both wrong since the module's first commit on every Spark version, invisible to mvn compile, and only found because something finally executed the code: (1) HsmUdfExtension originally took SparkSessionExtensions as a constructor argument, which compiles fine but Spark's own reflection code (confirmed byte-for-byte identical between Spark 3.5.1 and 4.2.0 via javap) calls Class.getConstructor() with zero args, casts the result to scala.Function1, and calls .apply(extensions) on it -- a constructor that takes an argument is simply never found, and Spark silently skips the extension with a warning instead of failing loudly; fixed by implementing Spark's own SparkSessionExtensionsProvider (a Function1<SparkSessionExtensions,BoxedUnit> marker interface built for exactly this) with a no-arg constructor. (2) Converting the UDF result Column back to an Expression via ExpressionUtils.expression(...) compiles fine and looks symmetric with the argument-direction ExpressionUtils.column(...), but produces an Unevaluable ColumnNodeExpression wrapper that throws '[INTERNAL_ERROR] Cannot generate code for expression' the instant Spark tries to codegen it, since that method is meant for Spark's own Column pipeline where a later Analyzer rule resolves the wrapper away -- code injected directly via injectFunction runs after that rule already had its chance; fixed by calling ColumnNodeToExpressionConverter directly, which performs that resolution immediately instead of deferring it. HsmUdfRegistration (the stable public-UDFRegistration-API path) needed no fixes at all, in keeping with its whole reason for existing as the lower-risk alternative. Remaining gap, unchanged: no real Spark cluster or live hsm-core-service exercised together in one run -- HsmCryptoClient itself (what both UDFs delegate to) was already separately live-verified end-to-end against a real hsm-core-service during hsm-crypto-client's own build, so what's left is specifically cluster classpath/config delivery, not encrypt/decrypt correctness.

items.item: hsm-spark-adapter: fixed a real deployability gap -- module built a thin jar, docs claimed a fat one
items.notes: Caught while preparing the final file-to-deploy list for hsm-spark-adapter: SPARK_ADAPTER.md's deployment section already claimed the built jar included hsm-crypto-client/bc-fips/nimbus-jose-jwt/jackson-databind, but the pom.xml had no shade/assembly plugin at all -- mvn package produced a 9.5KB jar containing only com.hsm.spark.* classes, nothing else, which would have failed with NoClassDefFoundError on every executor of a real deployment following the doc as written. Fixed by adding maven-shade-plugin (new to this repo -- every other module here ships either a plain library jar consumed via Maven coordinates, or a Spring Boot app via spring-boot-maven-plugin's repackage, neither of which applies to a non-Spring jar meant for spark.jars/a container image). Relocated io.netty inside the shaded jar to com.hsm.spark.shaded.io.netty: azure-identity (an hsm-crypto-client dependency, for the AZURE_AD auth mode) pulls Netty 4.1.x while this module's Spark 4.2.0 pin needs 4.2.x, and this was not a hypothetical concern -- assembling an unrelocated flat classpath for this module's own live-verification run hit exactly this collision, with Maven's nearest-wins mediation picking the wrong netty-transport-classes-kqueue version and breaking SparkContext's own RPC layer at startup with a NoClassDefFoundError. Jackson deliberately left unrelocated: Spark 4.2.0 itself depends on jackson-databind 2.21.2, a patch release of the exact 2.21.x line this module already pins (2.21.4), so no real collision risk, and relocating a library HsmCryptoClient calls directly (ObjectMapper et al.) risks breaking annotation-based reflection for no benefit. Re-verified with the exact same live-execution method used throughout this round: hsm_encrypt/hsm_decrypt registered and hsm_decrypt(...) executed through real SQL parsing, Catalyst analysis, and whole-stage codegen, using ONLY the single shaded jar plus Spark's own classpath -- no separately-listed dependency jars -- confirming the one-jar deployment story actually holds, not just that it compiles. Resulting jar is ~37MB, almost entirely netty-tcnative-boringssl-static's per-platform native binaries pulled in transitively, not this module's own code.

items.item: mTLS as a fourth, optional authentication mechanism, live-verified end to end
items.notes: Follow-up to a design discussion prompted by a security reviewer's threat -- a bulk-client/Spark-executor JVM's memory being dumped to extract cached plaintext DEKs -- which surfaced mTLS as a topic worth revisiting even though AUTHORIZATION.md had earlier recorded it as considered-and-rejected in favor of self-issued JWT (SELF_SIGNED_JWT). This round confirmed mTLS does NOT address that memory-exposure threat (it authenticates the network connection, not what a legitimate caller does with data afterward) but built it anyway as a genuinely optional fourth mechanism, coexisting with STATIC/AZURE_AD/SELF_SIGNED_JWT rather than replacing any of them, differing from the original rejected design in exactly that way. New V13 migration adds app_registrations.mtls_cert_fingerprint (SHA-256 of the DER-encoded cert, not the cert itself); new POST /admin/apps/mtls-cert admin endpoint (same provision_app_keys scope as POST /admin/apps/keys -- another authentication-trust-boundary credential, not a new blast-radius category), computing and storing the fingerprint server-side at write time. New MtlsServerConfig configures the embedded Tomcat connector (certificateVerification=optional, i.e. Tomcat's 'want' not 'need') with a new PermissiveClientTrustManager that accepts any client certificate at the TLS handshake -- self-signed certs (this design's expected shape, same fingerprint-pinned trust model as SSH host-key pinning) have no CA to chain-validate, so real identity validation happens afterward in new MtlsAppIdAuthenticationFilter, which resolves the caller from X-App-ID, looks up that app's registered fingerprint, and compares it against the actually-presented certificate -- a mismatch is rejected outright (401), never silently passed through, since presenting a certificate is an explicit choice to authenticate via mTLS. A request with no certificate at all skips this filter entirely and falls through unchanged to the existing JwtAppIdAuthenticationFilter (given a one-line early-exit guard: skip if SecurityContext already has an Authentication, letting an earlier successful mTLS auth pre-empt it) -- this is what makes the whole mechanism genuinely optional rather than a breaking change, gated overall by a new hsm.security.mtls-enabled flag (default false) that keeps every new bean out of the context entirely when off. Client side: a fourth SvcConfig.AuthMode (MTLS) in hsm-crypto-client; HsmCryptoClient.Builder.mtls(certPem, keyPem) builds an in-memory PKCS12 keystore from a bare PEM cert/key pair (new MtlsSupport helper) rather than requiring a Java keystore file, keeping the same bare-PEM convention every other credential in this module uses; SvcClient sends no Authorization header at all in this mode, since identity was already established at the handshake. hsm-spark-adapter gained matching spark.hsm.mtlsCertPath/mtlsKeyPath config keys in HsmSparkConfig, same Secret-mounted-file-path convention as the other three modes. Live-verified end to end against a real running instance with a real self-signed server keystore and real client certificates (openssl-generated, not mocked): a registered client certificate with NO Authorization header succeeded (pure mTLS auth, both via curl and via the actual HsmCryptoClient.builder().mtls(...) Java code path, not just curl); the same app_id with no certificate at all, using its existing static demo token, still succeeded unchanged (confirms 'optional' is real, not just documented); a different, unregistered certificate was correctly rejected with 401 'Client certificate not recognized for this app_id'; a certificate presented without the required X-App-ID header was correctly rejected with 401. One real-world gotcha surfaced and resolved during this verification: Tomcat logs a warning that TLS 1.3's JSSE implementation doesn't support post-handshake authentication and is 'incompatible with optional certificate authentication' -- tested directly rather than assumed away, and confirmed a non-issue for this design specifically, since Tomcat requests the client certificate as part of the initial handshake (client-auth=want at the connector level, not a later per-resource request), which TLS 1.3's normal CertificateRequest flow handles without needing PHA at all. New AdminMtlsCertTest (hsm-core-service, real SpringBootTest + H2, real keytool-generated certificate, not a hand-built ASN.1 fixture) covers registration, fingerprint computation, unknown-app-id 404, unparseable-cert 422, and wrong-scope-caller 403. helm/hsm-core-service and helm/hsm-bulk-service (the second release of the same image) both gained an MTLS_ENABLED config toggle (default false), documented as needing additional setup (a server keystore Secret, and a liveness/readiness probe scheme change to HTTPS) beyond the flag itself if actually turned on -- neither of those additional pieces is wired by this round, deliberately, since the feature stays off by default.

items.item: DEK memory-exposure hardening: bounded/TTL-evicting cache + JVM anti-dump flags
items.notes: Direct response to the same reviewer threat that prompted the mTLS work above (a bulk-client/Spark-executor JVM's memory dumped to extract cached plaintext DEKs) -- and to a correction from that same discussion: an earlier answer had listed DEK rotation as a partial mitigation for this threat, which turned out to be wrong on inspection of the actual code. RotationService.rekey() unwraps the old EDEK and re-wraps the identical dekBytes under a new KEK -- confirmed via the code, not assumed -- so KEK rotation never touches DEK material at all. NamedDekRotationScheduler does mint a genuinely fresh DEK, but the retired EdekRecord row is kept (RotationStatus.ROTATED), not deleted, since every already-issued ciphertext token still references its edek_id and must stay decryptable -- so a DEK's ability to decrypt everything already encrypted with it is permanent regardless of rotation, and a caller already holding that DEK cached client-side keeps using it for new writes too, since rotation has no server-to-client push/invalidation. Rotation was corrected out of the mitigation list rather than left standing. What actually shipped instead: new DekCache<K,V> (hsm-crypto-client) replaces the plain unbounded ConcurrentHashMap HsmCryptoClient previously used for both its encrypt-by-dekName and decrypt-by-edek_id caches -- bounded by maxSize (default 1000) and TTL (default 30 minutes), zeroing a DEK's bytes the moment it's evicted for either reason, not just at an eventual close(). A background sweeper (one daemon thread per HsmCryptoClient instance, 60-second interval) proactively zeroes expired entries even if never accessed again, closing the gap a purely lazy on-read check would leave open for a dekName a caller stops using but never explicitly evicts. Generic over a value type V (not just raw DEK bytes) with a caller-supplied extractor function, since the encrypt-side cache needs to hold an edek_id alongside the DEK, not the DEK alone -- the decrypt-side cache uses Function.identity() for the same class where V is already just bytes. Eviction concurrency uses ConcurrentHashMap's own compare-and-remove (remove(key, value)) rather than a separate insertion-order structure, specifically to avoid a real correctness bug caught during design (not just at review): a naive parallel queue can go stale when a key is refreshed after expiry, causing eviction to zero a DEK that was actually just re-issued and is still in active use. 11 new unit tests (DekCacheTest) cover reuse-without-reissue, TTL expiry with zeroing, the background-sweep path independent of access, max-size eviction that never exceeds the bound across many inserts, zero-on-clear, the generic-value-type/extractor path, a failed loader leaving the cache usable for the next call, and -- the one hardest to get right without a real concurrency test -- 20 threads racing on one key only ever invoking the loader once. Builder gained .dekCacheMaxSize(int)/.dekCacheTtl(Duration) for callers who need different bounds than the defaults. Separately, Dockerfile.hsm-bulk-client (the one Dockerfile in this repo that actually runs HsmCryptoClient's caching as a long-running-ish process; hsm-spark-adapter has no Dockerfile of its own, so the equivalent spark.executor.extraJavaOptions guidance was documented in SPARK_ADAPTER.md instead) now passes -XX:-HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError (HotSpot's own default already, set explicitly so no inherited override can silently re-enable it) and -XX:+DisableAttachMechanism (blocks jmap/jcmd-style live heap dumping via the standard JVM attach API -- the easiest way to pull a dump from a process with mere process-level access, short of a full OS-level core dump, which a shell-less distroless image can't itself defend against; that gap is named explicitly rather than papered over, with a pointer to the OS/container-level guidance this Dockerfile can't enforce on its own). None of this closes the threat entirely -- see AUTHORIZATION.md's 'mTLS does not address client-side DEK memory exposure' for the honest remaining gap (a DEK dumped during its live window, however short, is still fully exposed; only a hardware-protected client-side enclave or eliminating client-side DEK caching entirely would close that, and either would reverse the exact performance tradeoff this design exists to make) -- this round narrows the exposure window and raises the bar to actually reach it, which is what was asked for, not a claim of full closure.

items.item: AZURE_AD auth: client-secret credential support ported to all three buildCredential() copies
items.notes: Surfaced during a manual, real (non-K8s) AZURE_AD verification of hsm-bulk-client: az login worked, but setting AZURE_CLIENT_ID/AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET/AZURE_TENANT_ID directly did not -- AzureAdTokenProvider.buildCredential() (hsm-crypto-client) checked AZURE_CLIENT_ID alone and routed straight into ManagedIdentityCredentialBuilder before ever reaching DefaultAzureCredentialBuilder's own EnvironmentCredential (the real client-secret path), so setting a client secret was silently ignored and the call fell through to Managed Identity's IMDS endpoint, which only exists on Azure-hosted compute and just fails/times out anywhere else (a laptop, a non-Azure VM, this manual verification run). Checked whether this class of fix already existed elsewhere in the repo before writing new logic: AzureKeyVaultKekClient.buildCredential() (hsm-core-service, Key Vault access) already had it -- an explicit ClientSecretCredentialBuilder branch, checked before the Managed Identity fallback specifically because 'a caller who set a client secret clearly intends to use it, not fall through to node-identity resolution'. The other two sibling copies (AdlsFileStore, AzureBlobFileStore -- both hsm-bulk-client, ADLS/Blob file-store credential resolution) had the identical bug, unfixed. Ported the same branch (same order: Workload Identity -> explicit client secret -> Managed Identity -> DefaultAzureCredential) into all three, via AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET env var directly (no job.yml/HsmProperties config field for it in these three, matching their existing pure-env-var convention -- unlike AzureKeyVaultKekClient, which layers config-object/JWT-claim fallbacks on top for its own core-service-side purposes). Verified via mvn compile across hsm-crypto-client and hsm-bulk-client -- no dedicated unit test added since TokenCredential resolution itself has no local seam to test without a real Azure AD tenant (the actual bug was only reachable by running against one); the fix was validated by re-running the same manual AZURE_AD verification that surfaced it.

items.item: RsaJwtValidator: comma-separated multi-value audience/issuer support
items.notes: Surfaced by the same manual AZURE_AD verification above: after getting a real token via az login, its aud/iss did not match hsm.jwt.audience/hsm.jwt.issuer (single exact-match strings) -- decoding both an SPN (client-secret)-acquired token and a user (az login)-acquired token for the same app registration showed genuinely different aud/iss formats (v1.0 endpoint: aud=client-id GUID, iss=https://sts.windows.net/{tenant}/; v2.0 endpoint: aud=App ID URI, iss=https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/v2.0 -- which format comes back depends on which credential path/library acquired the token, not who the caller is). RsaJwtValidator.validate() previously did a single .equals()/.contains() check against one configured value each, so only one token format could ever be accepted at a time. hsm.jwt.audience and hsm.jwt.issuer (HsmProperties.Jwt) now each accept a comma-separated list of exact values -- RsaJwtValidator.splitCommaSeparated() parses it into a Set once at construction, and validate() accepts a token whose aud/iss matches ANY listed value; still a strict explicit allow-list, not a pattern/wildcard match, and an unset value still yields an empty set that rejects every token (same as the old single-value ''/null default). Fixing this surfaced a second, independent bug in the same area: SelfIssuedRoutingJwtValidator (which peeks a token's unverified iss claim to decide whether to route it to RsaJwtValidator or SelfSignedAppKeyJwtValidator) did its own separate single-value .equals(configuredIssuer) comparison -- with issuer now a comma-separated list, that comparison would never match a real value inside the list, silently misrouting every genuine Azure AD token to the self-signed validator instead (which would then fail signature verification with a confusing, wrong-cause error). Fixed by reusing RsaJwtValidator.splitCommaSeparated() (made package-visible) for the same parse, then checking set membership instead of whole-string equality. 6 new unit tests (RsaJwtValidatorTest, real RS256-signed JWTs against an in-test keypair, publicKeyPem configured directly so no live JWKS endpoint is needed): single-value backward compatibility, v1-style aud/iss accepted when listed alongside v2-style, v2-style accepted alongside v1-style, an audience not in the list rejected, an issuer not in the list rejected, and the unset-value-rejects-everything case preserved. Full hsm-core-service suite (13 test classes) re-run afterward with no regressions.

items.item: hsm-spark-adapter: fixed a real BC-FIPS + shading incompatibility, bc-fips-2.1.1.jar must ship alongside the shaded jar
items.notes: Surfaced while proving out a genuinely independent, no-reactor local[*] SparkSession verification harness (a separate project with its own pom.xml, no <parent> back to this repo, spark-sql_2.13:4.2.0 resolved fresh + the built hsm-spark-adapter shaded jar added as a system-scope dependency) -- the approach itself was suggested as an alternative to a full standalone cluster, and confirmed to correctly sidestep an unrelated, real problem first: this reactor's root pom.xml imports netty-bom and forces a specific patched Netty version project-wide (for CVEs azure-sdk-bom would otherwise pull in), which also silently downgrades hsm-spark-adapter's own provided-scope spark-sql dependency's transitive Netty version whenever it's resolved through this reactor (mvn exec:java, or an IDE run configuration pointed at this module) -- breaking SparkContext's own RPC layer at startup with the same KQueueIoHandler NoClassDefFoundError this module's shading was built to avoid in the first place. A genuinely independent project, not inheriting that override, resolves Spark's own correct Netty version normally and starts cleanly -- confirmed via direct reproduction and fix. With that solved, a second, more serious, previously-undiscovered issue surfaced: hsm_encrypt failed with org.bouncycastle.crypto.fips.FipsOperationError: Module checksum failed the moment HsmCryptoClient's static initializer called FipsBootstrap.register() -> BouncyCastleFipsProvider's constructor. BC-FIPS validates its own FIPS module integrity at class-init time by checksumming its own packaged classes against a value computed at build time; merging bc-fips into any uber-jar (maven-shade-plugin's default behavior, which this module's own shaded jar did for every hsm-crypto-client dependency including bc-fips) breaks that checksum outright, regardless of whether bc-fips's own packages are relocated -- a documented, intentional BC-FIPS constraint (FIPS-validated jars must not be repackaged), not something to filter/exclude around. This is not a hypothetical test-only concern: the exact same shaded jar is what a real spark-submit deployment uses too, so this would have broken hsm_encrypt/hsm_decrypt in any real cluster deployment the moment a caller actually invoked them, not just in this local verification harness -- HsmCryptoClientHolder lazily builds the client (and triggers FipsBootstrap.register()) on first UDF call, not at SparkSession startup, so the shaded jar's SparkSessionExtensionsProvider registration would have appeared to succeed cleanly and only failed on actual first use. Fixed by excluding org.bouncycastle:bc-fips from the shaded jar entirely (hsm-spark-adapter/pom.xml, maven-shade-plugin's artifactSet/excludes) rather than trying to preserve its packaging inside the uber-jar. bc-fips-2.1.1.jar must now be added to the classpath as its own, untouched jar alongside hsm-spark-adapter-1.0.0.jar in every deployment (spark-submit --jars, spark.jars, container image, Kubernetes Operator spec.deps.jars) -- documented in SPARK_ADAPTER.md's deployment section, including a corrected note removing the now-inaccurate earlier claim that the shaded jar alone (no other dependency jars needed) was sufficient. Confirmed working end-to-end after the fix: real SparkSession, spark.sql.extensions=com.hsm.spark.HsmUdfExtension, hsm_encrypt/hsm_decrypt executing through genuine whole-stage codegen against a real hsm-core-service instance, encrypt-then-decrypt round-tripping the original plaintext -- via the independent-project verification harness, not spark-submit against a downloaded distribution (none available in this environment), but exercising the identical shaded-jar-plus-Spark-classpath shape any real deployment uses.

items.item: Live-demo diagram injection (generate_demo_index.py) rewritten to pure Java, source SVGs moved from repo-root docs/ into java/docs/
items.notes: Two real, previously-undiscovered problems in the earlier Python-based build-time injection step (see the 'diagram-sync' items above for that original work), both surfaced only when actually trying a containerized build rather than a local mvn package: (1) Dockerfile.hsm-core-service's build stage is maven:3.9.9-eclipse-temurin-21, which has no Python interpreter at all, so the exec-maven-plugin step invoking python3/generate_demo_index.py could never run inside that container; (2) docs/architecture-diagram.svg and docs/sequence-diagram.svg (the actual source-of-truth files the generator reads) lived at the repo root, one level above java/ -- but that Dockerfile's own build context is java/ (docker build run from that directory), and Docker's COPY can never reach outside its build context regardless of which language does the reading, so even a perfect non-Python rewrite would still have failed with a file-not-found. Both fixed together, deliberately, since fixing only the language would not have made the Docker build work: (a) the injection logic was ported to a small, real Java class, DemoIndexGenerator (com.hsm.core.build.DemoIndexGenerator, hsm-core-service/src/main/java), invoked via exec-maven-plugin's java goal (in-process, no subprocess spawned at all, unlike the old exec goal shelling out to python3) bound to the prepare-package phase -- deliberately after both process-resources (the default resource copy placing the checked-in template) and compile (so this class's own bytecode already exists), removing the fragile 'explicit executions run after implicit default bindings for the same phase' ordering the Python version's process-resources binding depended on, in favor of an unambiguous later phase. Files.readString/writeString default to UTF-8, which also permanently closes the earlier UTF-8-encoding bug class this same script hit on non-UTF-8-locale build hosts, rather than just working around it with an explicit encoding= parameter as the Python fix did. (b) architecture-diagram.svg and sequence-diagram.svg were moved from the repo-root docs/ into java/docs/ (which already existed, holding this module's markdown docs) -- confirmed first, before moving anything, that this has zero effect on the live demo's actual served index.html: the generated output only ever contains the fully-inlined <svg>...</svg> markup, with no reference anywhere back to the source file's original path, so the external Python-based consumer project (which only ever reads the final index.html, never the source SVGs directly) is completely unaffected by where the source files physically live. Dockerfile.hsm-core-service updated with a new COPY docs docs line (after the existing COPY hsm-core-service/src hsm-core-service/src) so the build context now actually contains them. generate_demo_index.py deleted; hsm.python.executable Maven property (added for the earlier python-vs-python3 environment-portability fix) removed as now-unused. Verified via a full local mvn package: byte-for-byte identical generated index.html (87979 chars, same figure the Python version printed) to the previously-verified-correct output, zero leftover @@ markers, CLIENTS label count still exactly 2 (no reintroduction of the earlier header/body duplication bug), full hsm-core-service test suite (14 classes) still passing. Could not verify the actual containerized docker build end-to-end in this environment (no Docker daemon available here) -- the Dockerfile change and build-context reasoning were verified by careful reading and manual reasoning through Docker's own COPY/build-context semantics, not a live build; worth a real docker build as a final check before relying on this in a real deployment pipeline.

items.item: hsm-spark-adapter: HsmSqlScriptRunner, decrypted views over real JDBC-backed tables
items.notes: Direct response to a design review comment on HsmUdfExtension: the module stops one step short of useful on its own -- it hands a caller hsm_encrypt/hsm_decrypt and leaves them to hand-write per-column decrypt SQL themselves every time, when what a downstream consumer (an analyst, a BI tool) actually wants is a plain SELECT * FROM some_view. First design pass considered baking table/view definitions into HsmUdfExtension's own automatic, cluster-wide spark.sql.extensions registration path, but that was rejected: extensions apply identically to every application on a cluster, while table/view definitions are inherently per-job -- baking them into the automatic path would force every unrelated Spark application on the cluster to carry one job's view definitions. Correct next-review-round guidance settled on something much simpler than a bespoke table/column-mapping DSL: a conf file containing literal Spark SQL statements (typically CREATE TABLE ... USING org.apache.spark.sql.jdbc, then CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW ... hsm_decrypt(...)), split on a ;;; delimiter rather than a plain ; (a single semicolon can legitimately appear inside a statement itself -- a JDBC URL's query string, a quoted literal -- so it can't double as the separator; ;;; isn't valid SQL on its own, so it can never collide with real statement content). HsmSqlScriptRunner (hsm-spark-adapter/src/main/java) implements exactly this and nothing more: it has no knowledge of tables, views, or decryption specifically, it just runs each ;;;-delimited statement through spark.sql(...) in order -- the decrypt-view behavior comes entirely from ordinary SQL calling the already-registered hsm_decrypt, keeping this genuinely a generic script runner rather than a new crypto-aware abstraction. Explicitly invoked by a job (HsmSqlScriptRunner.run(spark, path)), same shape as the existing HsmUdfRegistration.registerAll(spark) explicit alternative, not part of the automatic extension path -- preserves the cluster-wide-functions/per-job-everything-else boundary. No JDBC driver dependency added to hsm-spark-adapter's own pom.xml, same reasoning hsm-bulk-client's own DB jobs already follow: the driver is whatever the real source/target needs, supplied by the job's own classpath at deploy time, not bundled into the adapter. Live-verified end to end, not just unit-level: a real H2-backed JDBC source table (customer_raw) seeded with a ciphertext actually produced by POST /encrypt against a real hsm-core-service instance, read via a real CREATE TABLE ... USING org.apache.spark.sql.jdbc statement, exposed through CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW customer_plain AS SELECT id, hsm_decrypt(ssn) AS ssn, zip, address, phone FROM customer_raw, queried back via SELECT * FROM customer_plain, and confirmed the decrypted ssn matches the original plaintext exactly -- via a new SqlScriptRunnerVerification class in the spark-verification-app companion project (repo root), the same genuinely-independent-of-the-java-reactor harness already used to verify HsmUdfExtension itself, so this ran through the real Netty-collision-free, BC-FIPS-shading-fixed classpath, not a simplified/mocked one.

items.item: hsm-spark-adapter: HsmThriftServerBootstrap, one self-contained process for Spark Thrift Server + registered functions + pre-created decrypt views
items.notes: Follow-up to HsmSqlScriptRunner: the natural way to expose decrypt views to BI tools/JDBC clients is a Spark Thrift Server, and the first-pass answer (config drives spark.sql.extensions registration, a separate manual beeline -f views.sql run after the server is up drives view creation) was correctly pushed back on as inelegant -- two disconnected steps, nothing guaranteeing the views exist before the first client connects, real operational mix-and-match. Investigated whether Spark exposes a real hook to embed Thrift Server startup behind one process instead, rather than assuming none exists: confirmed via actually resolving org.apache.spark:spark-hive-thriftserver_2.13:4.2.0 and javap-ing HiveThriftServer2 (not from memory) that it has a genuine public embedding API, HiveThriftServer2.startWithSparkSession(SparkSession, boolean) (and an older startWithContext(SQLContext) overload) -- exactly the hook needed: start serving the Thrift/JDBC endpoint on top of an already-built SparkSession, after that session has already had its UDFs registered and its startup SQL already run. HsmThriftServerBootstrap (hsm-spark-adapter/src/main/java) uses exactly this: builds a SparkSession the normal way (spark.sql.extensions=com.hsm.spark.HsmUdfExtension, same as any other deployment), optionally runs a startup script via HsmSqlScriptRunner (spark.hsm.startupSqlScript conf, optional -- omit to start with no pre-created views), then calls startWithSparkSession and blocks for the server's lifetime. Not a fork or reflection into HiveThriftServer2 internals -- entirely Spark's own supported public API. spark-hive-thriftserver added to hsm-spark-adapter/pom.xml as provided scope, same reasoning as spark-sql: any cluster capable of running Thrift Server at all already ships it, this class doesn't bundle its own copy. Live-verified end to end at the strongest level used anywhere in this codebase's Spark-adapter work so far: a real HiveThriftServer2 actually started via startWithSparkSession in the spark-verification-app companion project (a genuinely independent project outside the java/ reactor, same as every other hsm-spark-adapter verification), a decrypt view created by HsmSqlScriptRunner against a real H2 JDBC source seeded with a value from a real POST /encrypt call, then queried by a completely separate, genuine external JDBC client (org.apache.hive.jdbc.HiveDriver, added as its own test dependency) speaking the real Hive2/Thrift wire protocol over an actual network connection to localhost -- not an in-process spark.sql() call. Two real environment-assembly bugs surfaced and fixed during this verification, both about exec-maven-plugin's classpathScope, neither about HsmThriftServerBootstrap's own logic: (1) hive-jdbc pulls a legacy jdk.tools:jdk.tools system-scope dependency (a pre-JDK9 reference to tools.jar, which doesn't exist on JDK9+ at all) that had to be explicitly excluded to resolve on JDK 21; (2) classpathScope=compile (the value used by every other verification class in this project) excludes Hive's own runtime-only transitive shims, while classpathScope=runtime excludes this project's own system-scoped local jars (hsm-spark-adapter, bc-fips) entirely, since Maven excludes system scope from a plain runtime classpath -- classpathScope=test is the one scope that pools compile+runtime+system+test together, and is now what this specific verification run uses (the other two verification classes still use the default compile scope, since they don't need Hive's shims at all). Multi-vendor JDBC confirmed by design, not just documentation: HsmSqlScriptRunner and HsmThriftServerBootstrap both have zero JDBC-vendor-specific logic anywhere in them -- CREATE TABLE ... USING org.apache.spark.sql.jdbc is Spark's own generic datasource, so Postgres/Azure SQL/SQL Server/Oracle/MySQL all work identically, only the OPTIONS driver/url differ; added explicit per-vendor OPTIONS examples to SPARK_ADAPTER.md and views.sql.example rather than leaving that as an implicit claim.

items.item: hsm-core-service: close cross-app dek_name authorization gap -- global dek_name ownership + symmetric coarse/fine-grained encrypt+decrypt grants (V14)
items.notes: Found during testing: dek_name reuse on /encrypt had no cross-app ownership concept at all -- the unique index (idx_edek_current_name) was scoped (app_id, dek_name), so a second app could mint its own independent DEK under the identical name string another app already used, with zero grant check, silently accepted. Only /decrypt and /dek/unwrap were gated (via the pre-existing, decrypt-only, coarse-only app_decrypt_grants table); /encrypt, /encrypt/batch, and /dek/issue had no equivalent check on the encrypt side at all. Root cause and fix designed collaboratively across many turns before any code was written (two premature migration attempts were explicitly rejected mid-design -- 'we are just evaluating', 'am not favor of decrypt coarse-only?' -- until the model was fully settled). Final design, V14__add_scoped_grants_and_global_dek_name_ownership.sql: (1) dek_name is now globally unique -- the unique index moved from (app_id, current_dek_name) to current_dek_name alone, so whichever app's EdekRecord first holds a name becomes that name's permanent owner system-wide; a second app reusing it via /encrypt, /encrypt/batch, or /dek/issue without a grant now gets a hard 403, never a silently-independent DEK. (2) Grants are now symmetric across encrypt AND decrypt (previously decrypt-only), each with a coarse and a fine-grained tier, replacing app_decrypt_grants with two new tables consolidated via a scope discriminator column (mirroring the existing app_registrations.allowed_scopes free-text convention, deliberately not DB-constrained so a future scope needs no migration): app_grants (grantee_app_id, owner_app_id, scope) for coarse 'any resource' grants, and app_dek_grants adding dek_name for grants scoped to one specific name. Implemented as one unified AppRegistryService.isGranted(granteeAppId, ownerAppId, scope, dekName) called identically from EncryptionService/DekIssueService (scope=encrypt) and DecryptionService/DekUnwrapService (scope=decrypt); check order is same-app -> coarse grant -> fine-grained grant -> deny. Fine-grained checks use EdekRecord.getDekName() (permanent) not getCurrentDekName() (nulled on rotation), so a grant keeps covering a name's rotated/historical data. New POST/DELETE/GET /admin/dek-grants endpoints added alongside the now-scope-aware /admin/grants (both gated behind the existing grant authority); GrantRequest/GrantResponse gained a required scope field with no default (a clean-break API change -- existing dummy data and the one real caller, a documented curl example in ADMIN_OPERATIONS.md, were both updated in the same change rather than carrying a silent default forward). Governance-scope bypass on decrypt/unwrap left unchanged. Full hsm-core-service test suite green (85 tests, 0 failures) after fixing two pre-existing tests whose fixtures collided with the new global-uniqueness semantics (both reused a literal dek_name across different owning apps, which used to be legal and silently isolated per-app, and is now a real cross-app collision by design) plus four new tests added to EncryptDecryptIntegrationTest covering: cross-app reuse denied without a grant, allowed with a coarse grant, allowed with a fine-grained grant scoped to only that one dek_name, and unknown-scope rejection on /admin/grants. Docs updated: AUTHORIZATION.md (new #1d section with the full design writeup), ADMIN_OPERATIONS.md (endpoint table, timestamps section, direct-SQL section, curl examples), APP_ONBOARDING.md, DISASTER_RECOVERY.md, TIER3_POC_BUILD.md, and BULK_OPERATIONS.md (the exact gap this closes had already been flagged there as 'still open' in an earlier round -- marked resolved with a pointer to this migration). Follow-up (same round): the user asked for a real migration script rather than assuming a clean slate, explicitly accepting that pre-existing (accidental, ungranted) dek_name sharing across apps could legitimately break as a result. V14 was extended with two reconciliation steps that now run before it enforces anything new: (1) a pre-flight UPDATE resolves any pre-existing cross-app current_dek_name collisions using the same first-encrypt-wins rule (oldest created_at wins, NULLS LAST so an untimestamped row can never incorrectly win a tiebreak, edek_id as final tiebreak; losing rows get current_dek_name set to NULL, which only affects future reuse under that name -- dek_name, edek_id, and every already-issued ciphertext token are untouched, since decrypt/unwrap key off edek_id, never current_dek_name) -- otherwise the new global unique index creation would fail outright against any real deployment with an actual collision; (2) an INSERT...SELECT carries every existing app_decrypt_grants row forward into app_grants with scope='decrypt' before the old table is dropped, so no previously-granted app silently loses access. Caught a real bug during verification, not just reasoned through: the first draft's ORDER BY created_at ASC relied on the database's default NULL ordering for the tiebreak, which is NULLS LAST in real Postgres but turned out to be NULLS FIRST under H2's PostgreSQL compatibility mode -- confirmed by actually running the exact reconciliation SQL standalone (org.h2.tools.RunScript) against a synthetic pre-V14 dataset with a genuine three-way current_dek_name collision including one null-created_at row, which incorrectly let the untimestamped row win ownership over a row with a real, earlier timestamp. Fixed with an explicit NULLS LAST and re-verified the same way (correct winner, correct losers-set-to-null, unrelated rows untouched, both grant rows carried forward with scope=decrypt) before it was trusted. Full hsm-core-service test suite re-run clean afterward (85 tests, 0 failures), including regenerating a stale local demo H2 file whose Flyway schema_history still held the pre-edit V14 checksum. AUTHORIZATION.md #1d expanded with the full reconciliation writeup.
